note: Forbidding them to proceed to extremities is weakened to 'not to deal harshly'.
replacement: The Plataeans then sent a messenger to Athens, returned the dead to the Thebans under a truce, and set the city in order as the emergency seemed to require. The Athenians had been told of the affair right after it happened. At once they arrested every Boeotian in Attica, and they sent a herald to the Plataeans with an order not to proceed to extremes with their Theban prisoners until Athens had given instructions. Of course the news of the men’s death had not reached them. The first messenger had left Plataea just as the Thebans entered it, and the second just after their defeat and capture, so nothing later had come. The Athenians therefore gave their orders without knowing the facts, and when the herald arrived he found the men already dead. After this the Athenians marched to Plataea, brought in provisions and left a garrison there. They also removed the women and children and the men who were of least use.

note: 'This last' (the city wall) now reads as the Phaleric wall, making nearly five guarded miles of a four-mile wall.
replacement: While the Peloponnesians were still assembling at the Isthmus, or were on the march before invading Attica, Pericles, son of Xanthippus, one of the ten generals of the Athenians, saw that the invasion was coming. Archidamus happened to be his friend, and Pericles conceived that Archidamus might possibly pass over his estate and leave it unravaged. Archidamus might do so out of a personal wish to oblige him, or on instructions from Lacedaemon meant to set people against him, as had already been tried in the demand for the expulsion of the accursed family. So Pericles took a precaution. He declared in the assembly that, although Archidamus was his friend, the friendship would not be allowed to damage the state. If the enemy made an exception of his houses and lands and did not pillage them like the rest, he gave them up to the public at once, so that they could not bring him under suspicion. He also gave the citizens advice on their present affairs, in the same spirit as before. They should prepare for the war and bring their property in from the country. They should not go out to battle, but come into the city and guard it, and make ready their fleet, in which their real strength lay. They should also keep a tight rein on their allies. The strength of Athens came from the money that the allies’ payments brought in, and success in war depended chiefly on conduct and capital, so there was no reason for despair. Leaving other sources of income aside, the tribute of the allies brought in an average revenue of six hundred talents of silver. There were still six thousand talents of coined silver on the Acropolis, out of nine thousand seven hundred that had once been there; the money for the porch of the Acropolis, the other public buildings and Potidæa had been taken from this sum. This did not include the uncoined gold and silver in public and private offerings, the sacred vessels used in the processions and games, the Median spoils and similar resources, which amounted to five hundred talents. To this he added the treasures of the other temples, which were by no means small and could fairly be used. Indeed, if they were ever absolutely driven to it, they could take even the gold ornaments of Athene herself. The statue held forty talents of pure gold, and all of it could be removed. They could use this for their survival, but every penny of it must be restored. Such was their financial position, and surely it was a satisfactory one. Next, they had an army of thirteen thousand heavy infantry, besides sixteen thousand more in the garrisons and on duty at home in Athens. This was the number on guard at first, in the event of an invasion; it was made up of the oldest and youngest levies and of those resident aliens who had heavy armor. The Phaleric wall ran four miles before it joined the wall around the city. Of the wall around the city nearly five miles were guarded, though part of it was left without a guard, namely the part between the Long Wall and the Phaleric. Then there were the Long Walls to Piraeus, a distance of some four miles and a half, and the outer one was manned. Finally, the circumference of Piraeus together with Munychia was nearly seven miles and a half, but only half of it was guarded. Pericles also showed them that they had twelve hundred horse, counting mounted archers, sixteen hundred archers on foot, and three hundred galleys fit for service. These were the resources of Athens in each department when the Peloponnesian invasion was impending and hostilities were beginning. Pericles also urged his usual arguments for expecting a favorable outcome of the war.
